newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - U.K. PSBR expected to better govt target.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.K. PSBR expected to better govt target.

text.p: Britain's public debt is expected to be even lower than the government's official budget targets by the end of this financial year, according to a Reuters survey of economic forecasts.
But the economists polled took on average a gloomier view than the government on the outlook for Britain's public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) during fiscal 1997/98.
The mean of PSBR forecasts from 34 economists for the financial year ending April 5 was 25.7 billion sterling, inside the government target of 26.4 billion given last November.
But the experts were more pessimistic than the government for the 1997/98 fiscal year, making an average PSBR forecast of 20.5 billion compared with the government estimate of 19.2 billion.
"I think analysts are currently prepared to give the government the benefit of the doubt...but it will all go wrong again," said Steven Lewis, analyst with London Bond Broking.

The PSBR forecasts were collected as part of a wider quarterly survey by Reuters of British economic indicators, exchange and interest rates. Forty-two banks and research houses contributed to the survey, carried out between January 6 and 8.

The most pessimistic PSBR forecast for the current year was 29 billion sterling, and 24.1 billion for 1997/98, while the most optimistic put the debt well inside the government targets, at 21.1 billion and 13.3 billion respectively.
Analysts agreed that the PSBR would fall during 1997/98 as revenue increased and the winner of the general election, which must be held by May, tightened its fiscal policy.
They said the election winner would be forced to temper any spending plans because of the pressures of mounting debt.
"But as we go through 1998, we will return to the situation where the deficit mounts again," said Lewis.
The left-of-centre Labour party is well ahead of the ruling Conservatives in opinion polls.
Economists said the Labour Party's expected victory was not being seen as a factor in the expectations for expanding debt after 1997/98.
"The current government's spending plans are very tight. We worry about them being met and so there is room for caution," said Kevin Adams, analyst at BZW in London.

"The Labour party is going to face a stiff challenge in controlling expenditure, if only because of wage demands from the public sector which will expect them to be more generous than before," Adams said.
"The Labour party will be forced to sit down and look over the books...if the Labour party does not reach its targets it will not be because spending will run away with itself."
